Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit caused by Xanthomonas bacteria. Spreads fast in warm, humid, wet conditions.
organic_remedies: Spray neem oil solution (5ml neem oil + 2ml liquid soap per litre of water) every 7 days on leaves.
Apply copper-based organic fungicide (like copper oxychloride, OMRI-approved) as a preventive spray.
Remove and destroy infected leaves immediately to stop spread.
Avoid overhead watering; water at the base of the plant only, in the morning.
Rotate crops - do not plant peppers/tomatoes in the same soil for 2-3 years.
Use compost tea or cow-dung based bio-fungicide spray to boost plant immunity.
prevention_tips: Use disease-free, certified seeds.
Maintain proper spacing between plants for airflow.
Mulch around the base to prevent soil splashing onto leaves.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: This pepper plant leaf looks healthy with no visible signs of disease or pest damage.
organic_remedies: No treatment needed right now.
Continue regular monitoring for early signs of pests or disease.
Apply organic compost every 3-4 weeks to maintain soil health.
prevention_tips: Maintain consistent watering schedule.
Use organic mulch to retain soil moisture and suppress weeds.
Apply neem oil spray once every 2 weeks as a preventive measure.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target-like pattern) on older leaves, caused by the fungus Alternaria solani.
organic_remedies: Spray a mixture of baking soda (1 tbsp), neem oil (1 tbsp), and liquid soap (few drops) in 4 litres of water weekly.
Use compost tea spray to strengthen plant immunity.
Remove and burn/destroy infected lower leaves as soon as spotted.
Apply organic copper fungicide spray every 7-10 days during humid weather.
Improve air circulation by proper plant spacing.
prevention_tips: Practice crop rotation (avoid potato/tomato family in same spot for 2-3 years).
Water at soil level, avoid wetting foliage.
Remove plant debris after harvest to reduce fungal spores in soil.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Serious disease causing dark, water-soaked patches on leaves that quickly turn brown/black. Caused by Phytophthora infestans; can destroy entire crop if untreated.
organic_remedies: Immediately remove and destroy (burn, do not compost) all infected plants to stop spread.
Spray copper-based organic fungicide (copper hydroxide/oxychloride) every 5-7 days as soon as symptoms appear.
Use a garlic and chili extract spray as a natural antifungal.
Improve drainage - late blight thrives in wet, waterlogged soil.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water early in the day so leaves dry quickly.
prevention_tips: Plant blight-resistant potato varieties if available.
Ensure good spacing and airflow between plants.
Destroy volunteer potato plants and infected debris after harvest.

Potato___healthy.description: This potato plant leaf looks healthy with no visible signs of disease.
organic_remedies: No treatment needed right now.
Continue regular field monitoring, especially during humid weather.
Apply organic compost/vermicompost for continued healthy growth.
prevention_tips: Maintain proper irrigation - avoid waterlogging.
Practice crop rotation every season.
Use neem cake in soil as a natural pest deterrent.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Small, dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, stems and fruit caused by Xanthomonas bacteria.
organic_remedies: Spray neem oil + liquid soap solution every 7 days.
Apply organic copper-based bactericide as soon as spots appear.
Remove infected leaves and destroy them (do not compost).
Water only at the base of plants, avoid wetting leaves.
Use a diluted hydrogen peroxide spray (1 part 3% H2O2 to 10 parts water) on affected areas.
prevention_tips: Use certified disease-free seeds/seedlings.
Rotate crops - avoid planting tomato/pepper in same soil consecutively.
Stake or cage plants to improve airflow and keep foliage off the ground.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Brown spots with concentric rings on older/lower leaves, caused by Alternaria solani fungus.
organic_remedies: Spray neem oil solution every 7 days on both sides of leaves.
Use baking soda spray (1 tbsp baking soda + 1 tsp mild soap in 4L water).
Remove and destroy affected lower leaves promptly.
Apply compost tea to boost plant immune response.
Mulch around base with straw to prevent soil-borne spores splashing onto leaves.
prevention_tips: Rotate crops every 2-3 years.
Water at the base in the morning; avoid wetting foliage.
Stake plants for better air circulation.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Fast-spreading disease with dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves and fruit rot, caused by Phytophthora infestans. Can destroy the crop within days in humid weather.
organic_remedies: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately (burn, do not compost).
Spray organic copper fungicide every 5-7 days at first sign of disease.
Use garlic-chili extract spray as a natural antifungal booster.
Improve soil drainage and avoid overhead watering.
Apply Bacillus subtilis based organic bio-fungicide as a preventive measure.
prevention_tips: Choose blight-resistant tomato varieties.
Ensure wide spacing and staking for airflow.
Avoid working in the garden when foliage is wet to prevent spreading spores.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with olive-green/grayish mold on the underside, caused by Passalora fulva fungus. Common in humid greenhouse conditions.
organic_remedies: Improve ventilation - increase spacing and prune lower leaves.
Spray neem oil or potassium bicarbonate solution every 7 days.
Reduce humidity by watering early in the day at the base of plants.
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves.
Apply compost tea to strengthen plant defenses.
prevention_tips: Avoid overcrowding plants.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers.
Ventilate greenhouses/polyhouses regularly.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Small circular spots with dark borders and gray centers on lower leaves, caused by Septoria lycopersici fungus.
organic_remedies: Remove infected lower leaves immediately.
Spray neem oil or copper-based organic fungicide every 7-10 days.
Apply a baking soda + horticultural oil spray weekly.
Mulch soil to prevent fungal spores splashing onto leaves during rain/watering.
Use compost tea to improve overall plant health.
prevention_tips: Rotate crops each season.
Water at the base, keep foliage dry.
Clean up and destroy plant debris after harvest.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Tiny pests causing yellow stippling/speckling on leaves and fine webbing. Thrives in hot, dry conditions.
organic_remedies: Spray a strong jet of water on the underside of leaves to knock off mites.
Apply neem oil spray every 5-7 days, focusing on the underside of leaves.
Introduce natural predators like ladybugs or predatory mites.
Use insecticidal soap spray (mix mild liquid soap with water) directly on mites.
Keep plants well-watered - mites thrive on drought-stressed plants.
prevention_tips: Avoid excessive dust and dry conditions around plants.
Regularly inspect undersides of leaves for early signs of mites.
Maintain healthy soil moisture to reduce plant stress.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Brown lesions with concentric target-like rings on leaves, stems and fruit, caused by Corynespora cassiicola fungus.
organic_remedies: Remove and destroy infected leaves promptly.
Spray neem oil or copper-based organic fungicide every 7 days.
Improve air circulation through proper spacing and pruning.
Apply compost tea to boost natural plant resistance.
Avoid overhead watering; irrigate at soil level.
prevention_tips: Rotate crops with non-host plants.
Remove plant debris after harvest.
Stake/cage plants to keep foliage off the ground.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Viral disease spread by whiteflies, causing upward curling and yellowing of leaves, stunted growth.
organic_remedies: Control whiteflies using yellow sticky traps around the field.
Spray neem oil regularly to repel whiteflies (main carrier of this virus).
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread.
Use reflective mulch (silver plastic) to repel whiteflies.
Introduce natural predators of whiteflies like ladybugs and lacewings.
prevention_tips: Use virus-resistant tomato varieties if available.
Keep the area free of weeds that host whiteflies.
Use fine mesh netting on nursery seedlings to block whiteflies.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Viral disease causing mottled light/dark green patterns on leaves, leaf curling, and stunted growth.
organic_remedies: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately - there is no cure once infected.
Disinfect tools and hands with soap/diluted milk solution between handling plants.
Avoid smoking or tobacco use near plants (virus can spread from tobacco products).
Control aphids using neem oil spray, as they can spread the virus.
Practice strict field sanitation and remove weeds that may host the virus.
prevention_tips: Use certified virus-free seeds.
Wash hands and tools before handling different plants.
Rotate crops and avoid planting in previously infected soil.

Tomato___healthy.description: This tomato plant leaf looks healthy with no visible signs of disease or pest damage.
organic_remedies: No treatment needed right now.
Continue regular monitoring for early signs of pests or disease.
Apply organic compost every 3-4 weeks to maintain soil health.
prevention_tips: Maintain consistent watering at the base of plants.
Use organic mulch to retain moisture and suppress weeds.
Apply neem oil spray once every 2 weeks as a preventive measure.
